## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates the ability to design crash-safe concurrent data structures for non-volatile memory, assessing understanding of flush semantics, recovery mechanisms, and performance tradeoffs under contention.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory programming model and hardware semantics
- Write-ahead logging and flush primitives (CLWB, SFENCE)
- Per-slot version counters to prevent ABA problems
- Recovery procedures and WAL replay
- Memory ordering and cache-line alignment for performance

## Design Choice: Open Addressing
Linear probing with open addressing is preferred for NVRAM due to superior cache-line alignment, which minimizes unnecessary writes to persistent media, simplified recovery logic without traversing linked structures, and the elimination of pointer overhead inherent in chaining implementations.

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests understanding of low-level synchronization, fairness, and memory ordering with a practical API.

## Key Concepts
- Ticket locking
- Atomic operations and memory_order semantics
- False sharing and cache-coherence effects

## Code Example
```javascript
// Pseudo-C: fair ticket lock (conceptual, not compilable)
typedef struct { _Atomic uint32_t next; _Atomic uint32_t owner; } tt_lock;
void tt_lock(tt_lock* l){ uint32_t my=atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&l->next,1,memory_order_relaxed); while(atomic_load_explicit(&l->owner,memory_order_acquire)!=my); thread_local_uint32 = my; }
void tt_unlock(tt_lock* l){ uint32_t my=thread_local_uint32; atomic_store_explicit(&l->owner,my+1,memory_order_release); }
```

This question evaluates candidates on practical memory management under contention, focusing on per-thread caches and lock-free synchronization paths.

## Key Concepts
- **Thread-local freelists** minimize lock contention by allowing each thread to allocate and free objects without synchronization
- **Lock-free global pool** using CAS (Compare-And-Swap) enables safe concurrent access without blocking
- **Batch refills** (128 objects) amortize synchronization costs across multiple allocations
- **64-byte alignment** and padding help prevent false sharing between cores

## Why This Is Asked
Tests mastery of crash‑mode semantics, NVM tooling, and low‑level synchronization. It probes data layout decisions, fence ordering, and recovery guarantees under power loss.

## Key Concepts
- Crash‑consistent queues on NVM
- Per‑slot sequence counters and ABA avoidance
- Fence/flush ordering and cache‑line alignment
- Recovery protocol after crash and in-flight slots
- Single‑producer, multi‑consumer design trade‑offs

## Code Example
```cpp
// Pseudo-code (high level)
struct Slot { uint64_t seq; char payload[P]; };
Slot *ring; size_t head, tail, N;
void enqueue(void* d){ auto t=tail; write_payload(&ring[t], d); ring[t].seq = t; mfence(); tail = t+1; }
void* dequeue(){ auto h=head; auto s = ring[h].seq; if(s==h){ auto d = read_payload(&ring[h]); ring[h].seq = h+1; mfence(); head = h+1; return d; } return NULL; }
```
